title: Pearl & Dean (Phil.) Corp. v. Shoemart
summary: The Supreme Court distinguished between copyright, patent, and trademark protections for advertising display units. A copyright over the engineering drawings does not extend to the actual physical product. To protect the product itself, a patent must be obtained.
doctrine: Copyright protection extends to the expression of an idea, not the idea itself. An engineering drawing may be copyrighted, but the copyright does not extend to the useful article depicted. To protect the physical product or industrial design, the proper remedy is a patent or industrial design registration.
fullText:
CORONA, J.:

The issue is whether a copyright over the technical drawings and intellectual creation of an advertising display unit gives the creator the exclusive right to manufacture and sell the display units themselves.

Copyright, in the strict sense of the term, is purely a statutory right. It is a right granted by a statute for the protection of literary, scholarly, scientific, and artistic works. A copyright protects the form of expression rather than the subject matter of the work.

There is a distinction between copyright and patent. Copyright covers the right to reproduce an original work, while patent protects the right to the useful invention. The copyright holder of technical drawings cannot prevent others from manufacturing the actual product depicted, unless a patent has been obtained.
